United States voting pattern

"Red state" and "Blue state" redirect here. For other uses, see [Red State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_State_(disambiguation) "Red State (disambiguation)") and [Blue State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_State_(disambiguation) "Blue State (disambiguation)").

[Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") (26 states)

[Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politician "Independent politician") (1 territory)

[New Progressive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Progressive_Party_(Puerto_Rico) "New Progressive Party (Puerto Rico)") (Republican affiliated) (1 territory)

[Non-partisan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-partisan "Non-partisan") (Republican affiliated) (1 territory)

Starting with the [2000 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_presidential_election "2000 United States presidential election"), the terms **red state** and **blue state** have referred to [US states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_state "US state") whose voters vote predominantly for one party—the [Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") in red states and the [Democratic Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") in blue states—in presidential and other statewide elections.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-latmpexp16-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-smithsonian12-2) By contrast, states where the predominant vote fluctuates between Democratic and Republican candidates are known as _[swing states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_states "Swing states")_ or **purple states**. Examining patterns within states reveals that the [reversal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sixth_Party_System#Scholarly_perspectives "Sixth Party System") of the two parties' geographic bases has happened at the state level, but it is more complicated locally, with [urban–rural divides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban%E2%80%93rural_political_divide "Urban–rural political divide") associated with many of the largest changes.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-ReferenceA-3)

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/119th_United_States_Congress_Senators.svg/500px-119th_United_States_Congress_Senators.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:119th_United_States_Congress_Senators.svg) Incumbent senators. Red and blue denote two Republican or two Democratic senators respectively. Purple states denote one Republican and one Democrat from the state. Light blue stripes denote one independent senator (who caucuses with the Democrats).

All states contain both liberal and conservative voters (i.e., they are "purple") and only appear blue or red on the electoral map because of the [winner-take-all](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plurality_voting "Plurality voting") system used by most states in the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-4) However, the perception of some states as "blue" and some as "red", based on plurality or majority support for either main party, was reinforced by a degree of partisan stability from election to election—from the [2016 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._presidential_election,_2016 "U.S. presidential election, 2016") to the [2020 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), only five states changed "color"; and as of [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election"), 35 out of 50 states have voted for the same party in every presidential election since the red-blue terminology was popularized in 2000, with only 15 having swung between [the 2000 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_presidential_election "2000 United States presidential election") and [the 2024 election.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election") Although many red states and blue states stay in the same category for long periods, they may also switch from blue to red or from red to blue over time.

## History of the color schematics

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History of the color schematics")\]

### Origins

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins")\]

The colors red and blue are also featured on the [United States flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_the_United_States "Flag of the United States"). Traditional political mapmakers, at least throughout the 20th century, had used blue to represent the modern-day Republicans, as well as the earlier [Federalist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federalist_Party "Federalist Party"). This may have been a holdover from the [Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War"), during which the predominantly Republican north was considered "blue".[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-polidata1-5) However, at that time, a maker of widely sold maps accompanied them with blue pencils to mark Confederate force movements, while red was for the Union.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-6)

Later, in the [1888 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1888_United_States_presidential_election "1888 United States presidential election"), [Grover Cleveland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grover_Cleveland "Grover Cleveland") and [Benjamin Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Harrison "Benjamin Harrison") used maps that coded blue for the Republicans, the color perceived to represent the Union and " [Lincoln](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Lincoln "Abraham Lincoln")'s Party", and red for the Democrats. The parties themselves had no official colors, with candidates variously using either or both of the national color palette of red and blue (white being unsuitable for printed materials).

There was one historical use, associated with [boss rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_boss "Political boss"), of blue for Democrats and red for Republicans: during the late 19th century and early 20th century, [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") county election boards used color-coding to help Spanish-speaking and [illiterate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy") voters identify the parties;[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-7) however, this system was not applied consistently in Texas and was not replicated in any other state. In 1908, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")_ printed a special color map, using blue for Democrats and yellow for Republicans, to detail [Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt "Theodore Roosevelt")'s [1904 electoral victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1904_United_States_presidential_election "1904 United States presidential election").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-8) That same year, a color [supplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supplement_(publishing) "Supplement (publishing)") included with a July issue of _The Washington Post_ used red for Republican-favoring states, blue for Democratic-favoring states, yellow for "doubtful" states and green for [territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States") that did not have a presidential vote.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-visthesa08-9)

### Contrast with color usage in other countries

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Contrast with color usage in other countries")\]

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/119th_US_Congress_House_Start.svg/500px-119th_US_Congress_House_Start.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:119th_US_Congress_House_Start.svg) Incumbent House of Representative members by state. The darker the shade, the higher percentage of members of that party. Dark blue and red are 100% members of the party. Purple states are evenly split.

The 21st-century association of colors in American politics is contrary to the long-standing conventions of [political color](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_color "Political color") in most other countries whereby red symbols (such as the [red flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_flag_(politics) "Red flag (politics)") or [red star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_star "Red star")) are associated with [leftist politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing_politics "Left-wing politics")[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-10) including countries with such governments, such as [Red China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), whereas blue is associated with [conservatism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-:0-11) As late as the 1990s, Democrats were often represented by red and Republicans by blue.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-latmpexp16-1) According to _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")_, journalist [Tim Russert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Russert "Tim Russert") invented these terms during his televised coverage of the [2000 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_presidential_election "2000 United States presidential election").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-12) The 2000 election was not the first during which the [news media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_media "News media") used colored maps to depict voter preferences in the various states, but it was the first time the current red–blue terminology was used. In previous elections, the color assignments or even the actual colors used were often different.

### History of current designations

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: History of current designations")\]

The advent of [color television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_television "Color television") in America during the late 1950s and early 1960s prompted television news reporters to rely on color-coded electoral maps, though sources conflict as to the conventions they used. One source claims that in the elections prior to 2000 every state that voted for Democratic candidates but one had been coded red. It further claims that from [1976](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_United_States_presidential_election "1976 United States presidential election") to [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election "2004 United States presidential election"), in an attempt to avoid favoritism in color-coding, the broadcast networks standardized the convention of alternating every four years between blue and red the color used for the incumbent [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States")'s party.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-visthesa08-9)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-13)

According to another source, in 1976, [John Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Chancellor "John Chancellor"), the anchorman for _[NBC Nightly News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Nightly_News "NBC Nightly News")_, asked his network's engineers to construct a large illuminated map of the United States. The map was placed in the network's election-night news studio. If [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), the Democratic candidate that year, won a state, it was lit in red whereas if [Gerald Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Ford "Gerald Ford"), the incumbent Republican president, won a state, it was lit in blue.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-latmpexp16-1) It was said that Roy Wetzel, then the newly appointed general manager of NBC's election unit, justified the color scheme of blue for Republicans and red for Democrats for a simple reason: "Great Britain. Without giving it a second thought, we said blue for conservatives, because that's what the parliamentary system in London is, red for the more liberal party. And that settled it. We just did it. Forget all that communist red stuff. It didn't occur to us. When I first heard it, I thought, 'Oh, that's really silly.'"[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-smithsonian12-2) The feature proved to be so popular that, [four years later](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_United_States_presidential_election "1980 United States presidential election"), all three major television networks used colors to designate the states won by the presidential candidates, though not all using the same color scheme. [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_News "NBC News") continued its color scheme (blue for Republicans) until [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-latmpexp16-1) NBC newsman [David Brinkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brinkley "David Brinkley") referred to the 1980 election map outcome showing Republican [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan")'s 44-state landslide in blue as resembling a "suburban swimming pool".[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-14)

Since the [1984 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_United_States_presidential_election "1984 United States presidential election"), [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_News "CBS News") has used the opposite scheme: blue for Democrats, red for Republicans. [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_News_(United_States) "ABC News (United States)") used yellow for Republicans and blue for Democrats in 1976, then red for Republicans and blue for Democrats in 1980, 1984, and 1988. In 1980, when [John Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_B._Anderson "John B. Anderson") had a relatively well publicized campaign as an independent candidate, at least one network indicated provisionally that they would use yellow if he were to win a state. Similarly, at least one network would have used yellow to indicate a state won by [Ross Perot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ross_Perot "Ross Perot") in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election") and [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election"), though neither of them did claim any states in any of these years.

By 1996, color schemes were relatively mixed, as [CNN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNN "CNN"), CBS, ABC, NBC, and _The New York Times_ referred to Democratic states with the color blue and Republican ones as red, while _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ and _The Washington Post_ used the opposite scheme.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-17)

In the days after the 2000 election, the outcome of which was unknown for some time after election day, major media outlets began conforming to the same color scheme because the electoral map was continually in view, and conformity made for easy and instant viewer comprehension. On election night that year, there was no coordinated effort to code Democratic states blue and Republican states red; the association gradually emerged. Partly as a result of this eventual and near-universal color-coding, the terms "red states" and "blue states" entered popular use in the weeks after the 2000 presidential election. After the results were final with the Republican [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush") winning, journalists stuck with the color scheme, as _[The Atlantic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Atlantic "The Atlantic")'_ s December 2001 cover story by [David Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Brooks_(journalist) "David Brooks (journalist)") entitled, "One Nation, Slightly Divisible", illustrated.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-18)\[ _[original research?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research "Wikipedia:No original research")_\]

Thus, red and blue became fixed in the media and in many people's minds, despite the fact that the Democratic and Republican parties had not officially chosen colors.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-19) Some Republicans argue the GOP should retain its historic association with blue, since most center-right parties worldwide are associated with blue. On March 14, 2014, the [California Republican Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Republican_Party "California Republican Party") officially rejected red and adopted blue as its color. Archie Tse, _The New York Times_ graphics editor who made the choice when the _Times_ published its first color presidential election map in 2000, provided a nonpolitical rationale for retaining the red–Republican link, explaining that "Both 'Republican' and 'red' start with the letter 'R.'"[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-20)

## Map interpretation

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Map interpretation")\]

There are several problems in creating and interpreting election maps. Popular vote data are necessarily aggregated at several levels, such as counties and states, which are then colored to show election results. Maps of this type are termed [choropleth maps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choropleth_map "Choropleth map"), which have several well-known problems that can result in interpretation bias. One problem occurs when [areal units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Areal_unit "Areal unit") differ in size and significance, as is the case with election maps. These maps give extra visual weight to larger areal units, whether by county or state. This problem is compounded if the units are not equally significant. A large county or state in area may have fewer voters than a small one in area, for example. Some maps attempt to account for this by using [cartogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartogram "Cartogram") methods, but the resulting distortion can make such maps difficult to read.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-CromleyMcLafferty2011-21)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-ArayaBreindl2011-22) Another problem relates to data classification. Election maps often use a two-class color scheme (red and blue), which results in a map that is easy to read but is very generalized. Some maps use more classes, such as shades of red and blue to indicate the degree of election victory. These maps provide a more detailed picture but themselves have various problems associated with classification of data. The cartographer must choose how many classes to use and how to divide the data into those classes. While there are various techniques available, the choice is essentially arbitrary. The look of a map can vary significantly depending on the classification choices. The choices of color and shading likewise affect the map's appearance. Further, all election maps are subject to the interpretation error known as the [ecological fallacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecological_fallacy "Ecological fallacy").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-23)

Finally, there are problems associated with human perception.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-senay-24) Large areas of color appear more saturated than small areas of the same color.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-senay-24) A juxtaposition of differing colors and shades can result in contrast misperceptions. For example, due to the [simultaneous contrast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrast_effect "Contrast effect") effect, the [Bezold effect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bezold_effect "Bezold effect"), and other factors, an area shaded light red surrounded by areas shaded dark red will appear even lighter. Differing shades of red and blue compound this effect.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-Birkh%C3%A4user-25)

Cartographers have traditionally limited the number of classes so that it is always obvious which class a color shade represents. Some election maps, however, have violated this tradition by simply coloring each areal unit with a red-blue mixture linked to voting ratio data—resulting in an "unclassified choropleth map". These "purple maps" are useful for showing the highly mixed nature of voting, but are extremely difficult to interpret in detail. The lack of clear classes make these purple maps prone to the problems of color perception described above. However, there are pros and cons to both classified and unclassified choropleth maps. Each tend to show some patterns well while obscuring others.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-Birkh%C3%A4user-25) All these facts should be taken into account when looking at election maps.

### Critiques

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Critiques")\]

The paradigm has been criticized on several fronts. Many argue that assigning partisanship to states is only really useful as it pertains to the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)"), as well as (more recently) the Senate, primarily a winner-take-all system of elections (with the exceptions of Nebraska and Maine).

The Democratic or Republican party of a particular state may have policies that depart—sometimes greatly—from those of the national party, sometimes causing that state to favor one party in state and local elections and the other in presidential elections. This is most evident in the [Southern United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_United_States "Southern United States"), where the state Democratic Party organizations tend to be more conservative than the national party, especially on social issues.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Likewise, Republicans have elected many statewide officeholders in states that vote strongly Democratic in presidential elections, such as [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland "Maryland"), [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont"), and [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey"), generally by running closer to the political center.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

The elections in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Arkansas "2004 United States presidential election in Arkansas") as well as [West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_West_Virginia "2004 United States presidential election in West Virginia") in 2004 were won by Republican President [George W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush "George W. Bush"), but Democrats at the time held all four [U.S. Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") seats and majorities of elected executive officeholders in those states, including the governorship of the latter. Similarly, [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Tennessee "2004 United States presidential election in Tennessee") was won by Bush in both 2000 and 2004, but going into 2004, its governor was a Democrat and both chambers of the state legislature were controlled by Democrats as well. The converse can also be true, as in the case of [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Maine "2004 United States presidential election in Maine"), which had two Republican U.S. senators, but Democratic presidential candidate [John Kerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Kerry "John Kerry") won the state's electoral votes. Likewise, [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Vermont "2004 United States presidential election in Vermont"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_New_York "2004 United States presidential election in New York"), [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Massachusetts "2004 United States presidential election in Massachusetts"), [Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Maryland "2004 United States presidential election in Maryland"), and [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election_in_Hawaii "2004 United States presidential election in Hawaii") all voted for Democrat Kerry by wide margins, but all had Republican governors at the time.

In his address before the [2004 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Democratic_National_Convention "2004 Democratic National Convention") in [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston"), [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") spoke on the issue of blue states and red states, saying: "The pundits like to slice-and-dice our country into red states and blue states—red states for Republicans, and blue states for Democrats. But I've got news for them, too. We worship an awesome [God](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God "God") in the blue states, and we don't like federal agents poking around our libraries in the red states. We coach [Little League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_League_Baseball "Little League Baseball") in the blue states and have gay friends in the red states. ... We are one people, all of us pledging allegiance to the [Stars and Stripes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_the_United_States "Flag of the United States"), all of us defending the United States of America."[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-keynote-26)

In April 2008, Republican presidential nominee [John McCain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McCain "John McCain") predicted that the [presidential election that November](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election") would not follow the red-state-blue-state pattern, saying, "I'm not sure that the old red state, blue state scenario that prevailed for the last several elections works. I think most of these states that we have either red or blue are going to be up for grabs."[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-27) Arguably, this eventually proved to be somewhat true, but not in McCain's favor as Obama won three "red" states that had not voted Democratic in many years, namely [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), and [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") along with a part of deep red [Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska "Nebraska"), via the state's (much less conservative as a whole) [second congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebraska%27s_2nd_congressional_district "Nebraska's 2nd congressional district"). Obama also came close to winning [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and [Montana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montana "Montana"), losing both by a small margin. The only deviations from the preexisting red-blue paradigm were all in Obama's favor. In the four presidential elections since 2008, Indiana and North Carolina went back to supporting Republicans. Virginia has continued voting for the Democratic presidential nominees (as well as increasingly electing Democrats at the state level), leading to its being reclassified as a blue state in recent years. Nebraska's 2nd district flipped back into the Republican column in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election "2012 United States presidential election") and [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election"), but supported the Democrats in [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election") and [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election").

## Purple states

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Purple states")\]

Main article: [Swing state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_state "Swing state")

[![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/2016_Presidential_Election_by_County_%28Red-Blue-Purple_View%29.svg/500px-2016_Presidential_Election_by_County_%28Red-Blue-Purple_View%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2016_Presidential_Election_by_County_(Red-Blue-Purple_View).svg) [2016 United States presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election") results by [county](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_(United_States) "County (United States)"), on a [color spectrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_spectrum "Color spectrum") from [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") blue to [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") red

A purple state refers to a swing state where both Democratic and Republican candidates receive many votes without an overwhelming majority for either party. Purple states are also often referred to as "battleground" states.

The demographic and political applications of the terms have resulted in a temptation to presume this arbitrary classification is a definite and fundamental [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_United_States "Culture of the United States") division. Given the general nature and common perception of the two parties, "red state" implies a conservative region or a more conservative American, and "blue state" implies a more liberal region or a more liberal American. But the distinction between the two groups of states is less simplistic. The analysis that suggests political, cultural and demographic differences between the states is more accurate when applied to smaller geographical areas.

Traditionally, the practice of designating a U.S. state as red or blue is based on the [first-past-the-post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First-past-the-post_voting "First-past-the-post voting") winner-take-all system employed for presidential elections by 48 of the 50 U.S. states and the [District of Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"). Electoral law in Maine and Nebraska makes it possible for those states to divide their electoral votes: winner-take-all both by congressional district and statewide.

Despite the prevalent winner-take-all practice, the minority party almost always gets a sizable vote, with the most strongly partisan states typically having 25% to 40% of the population vote for the losing party in a presidential election. Most states have strongly Democratic cities as well as strongly Republican rural areas.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-patheos1-28)

[Robert Vanderbei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Vanderbei "Robert Vanderbei") at [Princeton University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University "Princeton University") made the first _Purple America_ map after the [2000 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_United_States_presidential_election "2000 United States presidential election").[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-29) It attempts to represent the margin of victory in each county by coloring each with a shade between true blue and true red. Due to the general absence of overwhelming victories, this technique results in mostly shades of purple. After the [2004 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._presidential_election,_2004 "U.S. presidential election, 2004"), Vanderbei and then others made similar maps summarizing the results. Quickly thereafter, the term _Purple America_ entered the public lexicon as a way of stating that the United States is not as divided as the political pundits would have the people believe.

[Cartograms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartogram "Cartogram") developed by Gastner, [Shalizi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosma_Shalizi "Cosma Shalizi"), and Newman at the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan") provide another way to depict election results,[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-gastner2004-30) which change from a red-blue paradigm to one of shades of purple.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-patheos1-28)

Forty-four of the 50 states were consistent in voting for Donald Trump or his Democratic opponent in the [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election"), [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), and [2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election "2024 United States presidential election") presidential elections. The exceptions were [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona"), [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") – all of which voted for Trump in 2016, Biden in 2020, and Trump again in 2024; and [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada") – the only state that voted for the Democrats in 2016 and 2020 but voted for Trump in 2024. [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania") and particularly [Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan "Michigan") voted in [2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election") and [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election "2012 United States presidential election") for [Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") handily, as well as having supported the [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") nominee in every presidential election since [1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_United_States_presidential_election "1988 United States presidential election"), suggesting they are gradually becoming redder. Inversely, [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)") and [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona") had supported [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") presidential candidates for decades before [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election"), with Georgia last voting blue in [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_States_presidential_election "1992 United States presidential election") and Arizona in [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_United_States_presidential_election "1996 United States presidential election"). This suggests that [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)") and [Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona "Arizona") are gradually becoming bluer.

Some states did not switch parties in 2016, 2020 or 2024, yet are/were still relatively even and often considered swing states. These include [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Carolina "North Carolina"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), [Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio "Ohio"), [Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iowa "Iowa"), and [New Hampshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Hampshire "New Hampshire"). Occasionally, swing state maps might include [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine"), [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") and [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas"), which generally vote for one party ( [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), [Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine") and [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") generally [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)"); [Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas "Texas") generally [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)")) but still often see close elections.

Feelings of cultural and political [polarization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polarization_(politics) "Polarization (politics)") between red and blue states, which have gained increased media attention since the 2004 election, have resulted in increased mutual feelings of alienation and enmity.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-31) The polarization has been present for only four close elections (2000, 2004, 2016, and 2020). One trend that has been true for several election cycles is that states that vote Republican tend to be more rural and more sparsely populated (thus having fewer electoral votes) than states that vote Democratic. Polarization is more evident on a county scale with the growing percentage of the U.S. electorate living in "landslide counties", counties where the popular vote margin between the Democratic and Republican candidate is 20 percentage points or greater.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-33)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-34)

### Red-state/blue-state secession

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Red-state/blue-state secession")\]

Various editorials[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-41)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-42) have proposed that states of the U.S. [secede and then form federations only with states that have voted for the same political party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_divorce "National divorce"). These editorials note the increasingly polarized political strife in the U.S. between Republican voters and Democratic voters. They propose partition of the U.S. as a way of allowing both groups to achieve their policy goals while reducing the chances of civil war.\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\]

A 2021 poll found that 52% of Trump voters and 41% of Biden voters support partitioning the United States into multiple countries based on political party lines.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-43)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-44) A different poll that same year grouped the United States into five geographic regions, and found that 37% of Americans favored secession of their own region. 44% of Americans in the South favored secession, with Republican support at 66%; while Democratic support was 47% in the Pacific states.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-46)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-47)

## Demographics

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Demographics")\]

Although the [Electoral College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)") determines the [presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_election "United States presidential election"), a more precise measure of how the country actually voted may be better represented by either a county-by-county or a district-by-district map. By breaking the map down into smaller units (including many blue counties lying next to red counties), these maps tend to display many states with a purplish hue, thus demonstrating that an ostensibly blue or red state may, in fact, be closely divided. Note that election maps of all kinds are subject to [errors of interpretation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#Critiques).

### Urban versus rural

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Urban versus rural")\]

These county-by-county and district-by-district maps reveal that the true nature of the divide is between [urban areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_area "Urban area") and [inner suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_suburb "Inner suburb") versus [rural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rural_area "Rural area") and [exurban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exurb "Exurb") areas. In the 2020 election, most voters in most rural counties voted for Republican [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"). [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)"), [Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada "Nevada"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"), and [Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisconsin "Wisconsin"), all states Biden won statewide, are good examples of this with some exceptions. Inversely, in solidly red states, most voters in most urban counties voted for Democrat [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"); good examples for this would be [Orleans Parish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans"), [Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisiana "Louisiana"), and [Davidson County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davidson_County,_Tennessee "Davidson County, Tennessee"), [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") (the locations of major U.S. cities [New Orleans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans "New Orleans") and [Nashville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee "Nashville, Tennessee"), respectively). Both provided Biden with double-digit margins of victory over Trump. An even more detailed precinct-by-precinct breakdown demonstrates that in many cases, large cities voted for Biden, and their suburbs were divided.

## Reaction

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Reaction")\]

### United States

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: United States")\]

The "Democratic blue" and "Republican red" color scheme is now part of the lexicon of American journalism.

Neither party national committee has officially accepted these color designations, though informal use by each party is becoming common. Both parties have since adopted logos that use their respective colors (a blue "D" for Democrats[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-48) and a red "GOP" for Republicans). [National conventions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_presidential_nominating_convention "United States presidential nominating convention") for both major parties increasingly feature the parties' respective colors, from the colors emphasized on convention podiums to the color conventioneers can be seen wearing on the delegate floor. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee also alluded to the color scheme when it launched a national "Red to Blue Program" in 2006.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-49)

The scheme has found acceptance and implementation from the U.S. federal government as the [Federal Election Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Election_Commission "Federal Election Commission") report for the [2004 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_United_States_presidential_election "2004 United States presidential election") uses the red-Republican and blue-Democratic scheme for its electoral map.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-50)

### International

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: International")\]

The choice of colors in this divide may appear counter-intuitive to non-American observers, as in most countries, red is associated with [socialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialism "Socialism"), [communist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism"), or [social democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_democracy "Social democracy") parties, while blue is associated with [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism "Conservatism") (especially [liberal conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_conservatism "Liberal conservatism")) parties. For example, the major center-right conservative parties in the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_United_Kingdom "Politics of the United Kingdom"), [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Canada "Politics of Canada"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Australia "Politics of Australia"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_New_Zealand "Politics of New Zealand"), [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Brazil "Politics of Brazil"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Italy "Politics of Italy"), [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Spain "Politics of Spain"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_France "Politics of France") and [Bavaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_Bavaria "Politics of Bavaria"), all use blue or its shades (whether officially or unofficially) whereas the major socialist, communist, or social democratic parties in each country are associated with red (orange in Canada). If the U.S. followed such a pattern, blue would be used for the Republicans and red for the Democrats. However, the current U.S. scheme has become so ingrained in the American election system that foreign sources who cover U.S. elections, such as the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), _[Der Spiegel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")_ and _[El Mundo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Mundo_(Spain) "El Mundo (Spain)")_ follow with the red-Republican, blue-Democratic scheme for U.S. elections.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-52)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-53)

## Australian usage

\[ [edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Red_states_and_blue_states&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Australian usage")\]

In Australia, the center-right [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_of_Australia "Liberal Party of Australia") uses the color blue, while the center-left [Labor Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Labor_Party "Australian Labor Party") uses the color red. The formal alliance between the two main center-right political parties in Australia, the Liberal Party and [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_of_Australia "National Party of Australia")), known as the [Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_(Australia) "Coalition (Australia)"), also uses blue (although the National Party itself uses dark green). While the terminology used in the United States is sometimes used in Australia, the terms "Liberal state" (or "Coalition state") and "Labor state" are generally used instead.

As the Coalition is dominant in regional and rural areas, states where over 40% of the population live outside the state capital typically have higher numbers of Coalition supporters.

However, state politics and federal politics are separate and many states vote for different parties in state and federal elections. While [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia") has a Labor government, federally the state has almost always voted for the Coalition, although has shifted to Labor more recently on both a state and federal level. The [Northern Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Territory "Northern Territory"), which also has a Labor government, has also historically voted primarily for the Coalition. [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania "Tasmania") has also been an important state for both parties over the past 50 years because, of the five Tasmanian seats in the [House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_House_of_Representatives "Australian House of Representatives"), there have been times where one party has won all five of them. As of the [2022 Australian federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Australian_federal_election "2022 Australian federal election"), the Liberals have two Tasmanian seats ( [Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Bass "Division of Bass") and [Braddon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Braddon "Division of Braddon")), as does Labor ( [Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Franklin "Division of Franklin") and [Lyons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Lyons "Division of Lyons")), the remaining seat ( [Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Clark "Division of Clark")) being represented by [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_politicians_in_Australia "Independent politicians in Australia") [Andrew Wilkie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Wilkie "Andrew Wilkie"). Queensland and Tasmania were considered the two states that delivered [Scott Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Morrison "Scott Morrison")'s unpredicted win at the [2019 federal election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Australian_federal_election "2019 Australian federal election") and both states are the only two where less than 50% of the population resides in the capital city ( [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane") and [Hobart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobart "Hobart"), respectively), which is important due to the Coalition's dominance in regional Australia.

Of the 29 federal elections held since [1949](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1949_Australian_federal_election "1949 Australian federal election"), Labor has won the federal two-party-preferred vote in Queensland just three times: in [1961](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1961_Australian_federal_election "1961 Australian federal election"), [1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_Australian_federal_election "1990 Australian federal election") and [2007](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Australian_federal_election "2007 Australian federal election") (when Queenslander [Kevin Rudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Rudd "Kevin Rudd") was leader of the Labor Party); and in Western Australia just six times: in [1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Australian_federal_election "1969 Australian federal election"), [1983](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_Australian_federal_election "1983 Australian federal election"), [1984](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Australian_federal_election "1984 Australian federal election"), [1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Australian_federal_election "1987 Australian federal election"), [2001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Australian_federal_election "2001 Australian federal election") (when Western Australian [Kim Beazley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Beazley "Kim Beazley") was Labor leader) and 2022. Conversely, in the [Australian Capital Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory "Australian Capital Territory"), which is dominated by national capital [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra "Canberra"), Labor has won the two-party-preferred vote in every election except the [1975 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1975_Australian_federal_election "1975 Australian federal election").[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_states_and_blue_states#cite_note-54)

In Australia, the leader of the party that forms government (wins a majority of seats in the House of Representatives) becomes [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Australia "Prime Minister of Australia"), who does not always win the primary vote or even the two-party-preferred vote (although the later scenario is rare for federal elections, last occurring in [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Australian_federal_election "1998 Australian federal election")) due to the voting system being [unproportional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation"). This happens in the United States as well.

**Red and Blue States 2024:** The terms "red state" and "blue state" emerged during the 2000 U.S. presidential election to describe states that predominantly vote for the Republican (red) or Democratic (blue) parties, particularly in presidential and statewide elections. States that swing between voting Republican or Democratic are called "swing states" or "purple states."

**The map will be updated as soon as the election results are out.** This Red and Blue States Map represents the results as of 2:00 AM on 06 October:

_**Red and Blue States Map 2024**_

Over time, these colour associations have highlighted broader geographic shifts in party bases. At the state level, there's a clear trend, but locally, the landscape is more complex, often marked by significant urban-rural divides. Generally, urban areas lean Democratic, while rural regions tend to favour Republicans. Despite these colour-coded trends, every state includes voters across the political spectrum; the red or blue shading often simply reflects the results of the winner-take-all electoral system that most states use in the Electoral College.

The continuity of red and blue designations over time reflects some level of partisan stability. From 2016 to 2020, for example, only five states switched parties in the presidential election, and as of 2020, 35 out of 50 states have consistently voted for the same party in every election since the red-blue terminology became widely used in 2000. This indicates a certain level of predictability in how states vote, although shifts do occur. For instance, between the 2000 and 2020 presidential elections, 15 states shifted party preference, showing that while some states have long-standing loyalties, others may experience periodic realignments.

A "red state" is characterized by the prevailing popularity and success of the Republican Party in elections. These states are predominantly situated in the South, Midwest, and Great Plains regions of the country. Marked by a conservative political orientation, red states emphasize principles such as smaller government, individual freedom, and lower taxes in their policies. The political landscape in these states is often shaped by substantial rural populations, influencing their attitudes and priorities.

Moreover, red states frequently boast a higher proportion of evangelical Christians and other religious conservatives. This demographic tends to lend support to socially conservative policies, including opposition to abortion and same-sex marriage. The distinctive combination of geographic location, political philosophy, and cultural factors collectively contributes to the characteristic identity of red states within the American political landscape.

### Swing States

Swing states, those that lack a consistent allegiance to either political party in national elections, stand as pivotal battlegrounds for presidential candidates. The outcome in these states can be the determining factor between victory and defeat in an election, prompting significant investment of campaign resources to influence voters. Navigating the dynamic electoral landscape requires constant scrutiny by presidential campaigns and political analysts. While past swing states can be discerned by examining historical vote closeness, identifying potential swing states in future elections demands a nuanced approach. Estimations and projections hinge on factors such as previous election outcomes, opinion polling, political trends, recent developments since the last election, and the strengths or weaknesses of the candidates in play:

Seven states have only one congressional district each, rendering congressional redistricting unnecessary. Four states employ [independent commissions](https://ballotpedia.org/Independent_commissions "Independent commissions") to draw the district maps. In two states, [politician commissions](https://ballotpedia.org/Politician_commissions "Politician commissions") draw congressional district lines. State legislative district lines are primarily the province of the state legislatures themselves in 37 states. In seven states, politician commissions draw state legislative district lines. In the remaining six states, independent commissions draw the lines.[\[3\]](https://ballotpedia.org/State_government_trifectas#cite_note-loyola_who-3) ##### 2010 As a result of the 2010 elections, 21 states had a change in trifecta status. Twelve of those states saw changes that would go on to impact the 2010 redistricting process. Details on the redistricting process in those 12 states can be seen below. - [In Alabama](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Alabama "Redistricting in Alabama"), the state legislature is responsible for drawing both congressional and state legislative district lines. - [In Colorado](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Colorado "Redistricting in Colorado"), the state legislature draws congressional district lines. Colorado's state legislative boundaries are drawn by a politician commission. - [In Indiana](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Indiana "Redistricting in Indiana"), the state legislature is responsible for drawing both congressional and state legislative district lines. The governor may veto the maps drawn by the legislature. - [In Iowa](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Iowa "Redistricting in Iowa"), an advisory commission drafts congressional and state legislative district boundaries. The state legislature retains final authority to implement district maps. - [In Maine](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Maine "Redistricting in Maine"), both congressional and state legislative district boundaries are drawn by the state legislature. An advisory commission is also involved in the process. - [In Michigan](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Michigan "Redistricting in Michigan"), congressional and state legislative district boundaries are drawn by the state legislature. - [In New Hampshire](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_New_Hampshire "Redistricting in New Hampshire"), congressional and state legislative district boundaries are drawn by the state legislature. - [In North Carolina](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_North_Carolina "Redistricting in North Carolina"), the state legislature is responsible for drawing both congressional and state legislative district lines. District maps cannot be vetoed by the governor. - [In Ohio](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Ohio "Redistricting in Ohio"), congressional district boundaries are set by the state legislature. State legislative district lines are drawn by a politician commission. - [In Oregon](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Oregon "Redistricting in Oregon"), the state legislature is primarily responsible for drawing both congressional and state legislative district lines. If the legislature fails to approve a state legislative district map, the secretary of state must draw the boundaries. There is no similar backup provision for congressional redistricting. - [In Pennsylvania](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Pennsylvania "Redistricting in Pennsylvania"), congressional district boundaries are drawn by the state legislature. State legislative district lines are drawn by a politician commission. - [In Wisconsin](https://ballotpedia.org/Redistricting_in_Wisconsin "Redistricting in Wisconsin"), both congressional and state legislative district boundaries are drawn by the Wisconsin State Legislature. ## Trifecta status by state (1990-present) The tables below display the partisan control of the governor's office and state legislative chambers in each state since 1990.
